draft.title: Persuasive techniques
card: a technique that works on a reader's feelings or sense of fairness. An appeal to fear or pity stirs emotion. An appeal to fairness says everyone deserves equal treatment.
words such as we, us and our. They place the writer and reader on the same side, as in "We all use this footpath".
a question asked for effect, not for an answer. "Would you let your child walk home alone?" pushes the reader to agree with the writer's answer.
words that make the other side look foolish, selfish or dishonest, such as "a few grumpy neighbours". This can turn readers against that side.
draft.remember: Persuasive techniques win readers over by using feelings, fairness, shared identity, questions and criticism of the other side.

a.q: A writer says, "We must protect our local pool for our children." Which technique is most clearly used?
a.why: The words we and our place the writer and reader together on one side. There is no question asked, no opponent criticised and no claim about equal treatment.
a.clue: Look at the small words we and our.

b.q: Priya writes in a school newsletter: "Surely every sensible parent wants cooler rooms?" What is the main effect of this sentence?
opts: It pushes readers to agree that the answer must be yes
It gives readers statistics about heat in classrooms
It shows the writer is calm and balanced about both views
It asks an expert to explain how heat affects learning
b.why: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, and the word surely suggests only one answer is sensible. It also hints that disagreeing makes a parent foolish. It contains no statistics or expert, and it is not balanced.
b.clue: Does the writer really expect an answer to the question?

b.best: It pushes readers to agree that the answer must be yes
